source_text: **(b) Restate the argument in its strongest reasonable form.** Write out the premises and conclusion as the speaker would accept them. Be concrete: - **Read hedges as hedges.** "Likely", "may", "should be investigated" and "I suspect" make a weaker claim than "proves" or "will". Judge the claim actually made, not a stronger one. - **Supply common-knowledge premises the speaker would accept.** If a step needs a premise that any ordinary reader takes for granted (drunk driving is dangerous; water boils when heated), assume it, even though it is unstated. Do not count its absence as missing evidence. **Common knowledge** means something an educated general reader would know without looking it up. If reviewers could reasonably differ on whether a fact is common knowledge, treat it as not common knowledge. - **Read recommendations as claims when they rest on a cause.** A recommendation whose only rationale is a causal effect ("so take vitamin D", "so close the school") counts as asserting that effect, and as asserting it as established unless it is hedged. - **Supply the most plausible unstated premise, not the weakest.** If two readings fit the words, use the one that makes the argument better. - **Treat stated defaults and procedural rules as such.** A burden of proof, a presumption of innocence, a null hypothesis, a house rule or a decision procedure tells you what to do when evidence is lacking. It is not a claim about what is true. - **Respect the conclusion's scope.** A conclusion about what to do, what to investigate, or what is probable is not a claim that the matter is settled. - **Keep the role of each statement.** An illustration, a joke or a figure of speech is not a premise unless the speaker relies on it. - **Excerpts of real texts.** If the passage is an excerpt and a condition fails only because support may lie past the excerpt boundary (the reply or the evidence may come in the next sentence or chapter), record at most possible issue and say what the full text would need to show. Do not import your memory of the full text as if it were in the passage. - **Contested readings.** For a well-known argument whose fallacy charge is disputed in the scholarly literature, name the classic charge, mark the row "contested reading", and give possible issue unless the passage's own words settle it. State the reading under which it is a fallacy.
